title: Ai At Work: Practice Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: Per the lesson "The 30-Day On-ramp: One Skill a Week, a Short Daily Practice", which two learning-science findings carry the design?
options: The spacing effect and the testing effect
The Pareto principle and the Dunning-Kruger effect
The Zeigarnik effect and the halo effect
The sunk-cost effect and the recency effect
questions.explanation: The lesson says both findings have been replicated for decades and that together they yield a training rhythm nearly matched to how human memory works.

questions.question: Which set of checks does Lesson 6 recommend before trusting AI output?
options: Check whether it sounds confident, reads smoothly, and is well formatted
Check whether it answers the actual question, is specific or vague, cites or hedges, and matches what you know
Check whether it is short, polite, and uses plain language
Check whether it agrees with your existing opinion
questions.explanation: Lesson 6's four checks: does it answer the actual question, is it specific or vague, does it cite or hedge, and does it match what you know.

questions.question: Which shorthand does the lesson give for the brief?
options: Ask, Check, Ship, Stop
Plan, Draft, Review, Send
Role, Task, Context, Format
Prompt, Iterate, Verify, Decide
questions.explanation: The lesson calls the brief the single most used product of the series and reduces it to the four-word shorthand of Role, Task, Context, and Format.

questions.question: Why does Lesson 14 say cleaning comes before analysis?
options: Because analysis is only as good as the table it runs on, and messy data produces confident wrong totals
Because cleaning is the only interesting part of spreadsheet work
Because the tool cannot read any messy data at all
Because cleaning is faster than analysis
questions.explanation: Lesson 14: garbage in, garbage out) except the garbage comes back looking polished. A messy sheet makes the tool silently skip text rows or count duplicates, producing a specific but wrong total.

questions.question: Lesson 12 distinguishes two distinct jobs. What are they?
options: Writing and proofreading
Editing (fixing what is there) and reviewing (checking before it ships)
Summarizing and translating
Generating and formatting
questions.explanation: Lesson 12 defines editing as the craft pass that makes a mostly-right draft better, and reviewing as the gate that checks whether it is safe to send. Mixing them up is how errors get through.

questions.question: The lesson measures one workflow on three axes. Which set does it name?
options: Cost, speed, and satisfaction
Volume, errors, and latency
Time saved, quality, and adoption
Revenue, retention, and risk
questions.explanation: The lesson replaces trust with numbers on exactly those three axes so the team can tell whether to keep the workflow, fix it, or drop it.

questions.question: What is Lesson 11's core division of labor between you and the AI tool?
options: You bring the facts and judgment; AI brings the fluent first pass
AI brings the facts; you bring the fluency
AI makes all decisions; you only forward its output
You do all the drafting; AI only fixes spelling
questions.explanation: Lesson 11's key line: 'You bring the facts and the judgment. AI brings the fluent first pass.' The user owns accuracy; the tool supplies the drafting.

questions.question: According to Lesson 1, what is the most accurate way to describe a large language model (LLM)?
options: A rules engine that follows pre-written instructions to produce answers
A giant statistical prediction machine that predicts the next most likely token
A database that looks up exact facts when asked a question
A deterministic calculator that always returns the same answer to the same question
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 describes an LLM as a giant statistical prediction machine that predicts the next token. It is not a rules engine, a fact database, or a deterministic calculator.

questions.question: Lesson 7 says a good prompt is not a wish) what is it?
options: A very long paragraph of background information
A brief, made up of four parts: role, task, context, and format
A single keyword that names the topic
A request phrased as a polite question with no detail
questions.explanation: Lesson 7's core idea: 'A good prompt is not a wish, it is a brief.' The four parts are Role, Task, Context, and Format, matching the template the lesson provides.

questions.question: What did the Harvard Business School entrepreneur study cited in Lesson 16 conclude?
options: AI advice improved performance for everyone equally
The tool did not improve performance on its own; high performers picked specific suggestions while low performers took generic ones
Low performers improved more than high performers
The tool's advice was identical to a human consultant's
questions.explanation: Lesson 16: the AI business advisor boosted high performers by 10-15 percent and lowered low performers by ~8 percent. The difference was which advice users chose to follow: the judgment was what separated them.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist on taking a baseline?
options: Because baselines are required for compliance reporting
Because you cannot claim a tool saves time unless you know how long the task took before the tool existed, and skipping this is the biggest reason time-saved claims fall apart
Because a baseline replaces the need for a quality bar
Because it means you can skip measuring after the change
questions.explanation: The lesson says you measure first, then change, then measure again, and the difference is your answer, with the skipped baseline named as the reason the time-saved claims collapse.

questions.question: What is the most-cited fix for a good meeting, according to the research Lesson 15 cites?
options: Having more people attend
Setting a clear agenda is the most-cited fix for making a meeting productive.
Recording every meeting
Shortening the meeting to 15 minutes
questions.explanation: Lesson 15 cites research where 67 percent of professionals named setting a clear agenda as what makes for a good meeting) a clear agenda is the single most-cited fix.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Measuring What's Working: Time Saved, Quality, and Adoption", what is a decision metric?
options: A number you would actually change your behavior on, as opposed to decoration
Any number that is easy to collect automatically
A metric that leadership has requested
The total number of tasks run in a month
questions.explanation: The lesson calls a count of tasks run decoration if you would keep running them regardless, and contrasts it with a number like drafting time dropping from nine minutes to five.

questions.question: Per the lesson "The Human-in-the-Loop Quality Bar: Standards and Review", what distinguishes review from editing?
options: Editing improves a draft, while review decides whether the draft is good enough to ship at all
Review is simply an extended round of editing
Editing is done by a manager and review by the author
They are two names for the same activity
questions.explanation: The lesson says you can edit a draft that is fine and you can review a draft you never touch, because review is the gate where your accountability lives.

questions.question: What example does Lesson 9 cite to show the real-world danger of invented output?
options: A 2023 lawyer who cited fabricated case law produced by an AI tool
A spreadsheet formula that returned a wrong total
A meeting transcript that misattributed a speaker
A marketing email with a broken image link
questions.explanation: Lesson 9 cites the 2023 lawyer who submitted fabricated case law generated by an AI tool, plus the Macquarie fake-reference experiment, to illustrate the stakes of invented facts.

questions.question: What distinguishes a placeholder in a template, as described in Lesson 10?
options: It is a fixed word that never changes between uses
It is a braced variable like {project_name} that gets filled in each use
It is a command to the model to add its own facts
It is a hard-coded date that stays the same
questions.explanation: Lesson 10 explains placeholders as braced variables (like {project_name}) that you fill in each time, sitting between a one-off prompt and a reusable template.

questions.question: How does the lesson define blast radius?
options: The number of teammates using the same tool
How much damage a wrong output can do, which belongs to the task rather than the tool
The size of the context window the task requires
The cost of the model call for the step
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts a wrong draft of a status summary with a wrong figure sent to fifty people and says the same tool can have a tiny radius on one task and a huge one on another.

questions.question: How does the lesson define cost?
options: Only the price of the AI subscription
Only the time you spend typing the prompt
Your time, the risk of a wrong answer, the effort of checking, and the downside if the tool is confidently wrong
The number of tokens the model consumes
questions.explanation: The lesson widens cost past money and says the real question is whether the tool does the task better and more cheaply than the alternative once you count the checking.

questions.question: In Lesson 1, how is an 'agent' defined, in contrast to a plain chatbot?
options: An agent is just another name for a single-turn chatbot
An agent is a model that takes multiple steps and uses tools to accomplish a goal
An agent is a model that has no tools and can only answer text questions
An agent is a pre-written automation that never calls any model
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 defines an agent as a model that takes multiple steps and uses tools, distinguishing it from a single-response chatbot. It also warns against 'chatbots in a trench coat' that are given a fancy name without real multi-step capability.

questions.question: What does the lesson draw from the testing effect, or retrieval practice?
options: Watching a training video is the most effective way to learn a skill
Re-reading documentation produces stronger learning than trying the skill
Actively using or recalling the skill on real work produces stronger learning than passively re-reading or re-watching, even though it feels harder in the moment
Retrieval practice only applies to rote memorization tasks
questions.explanation: The lesson says people underestimate the testing effect because easy re-reading feels more productive while it is happening, and it uses that finding to require daily sessions that use the skill on real work.

questions.question: Which prompting practice does Lesson 2 recommend to keep load-bearing facts reliable in a long conversation?
options: Put the most important instruction near the end and restate critical facts
Never repeat any instruction to avoid annoying the model
Keep every instruction at the very start and never restate facts
Ignore the total length of the conversation entirely
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 recommends placing important instructions near the end, restating load-bearing facts (like 'the contract is with Meridian'), and watching total length: using staged summarization for very long conversations.

questions.question: What is the 'golden rule' for testing whether your prompt is complete, per Lesson 7?
options: Send it to the vendor's support team for review
Show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context and see if they understand it
Rewrite it until it is shorter than one sentence
Check that every word is a keyword
questions.explanation: Lesson 7 cites Anthropic's golden rule: show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context: if they can't act on it, neither will the model.

questions.question: Lesson 6 describes an AI tool as what kind of colleague?
options: An infallible expert whose answers never need checking
A helpful but fallible colleague who writes fast, sounds certain, and has no idea what is true
A slow but always-correct researcher
A database that returns only verified facts
questions.explanation: Lesson 6 frames AI as a helpful but fallible colleague who writes fast, sounds certain, and has no idea what is true. Its answer is 'a draft of information,' not the truth.

questions.question: When comparing sources, what specific question does Lesson 13 tell you to ask the tool?
options: Where do these sources disagree, and what exactly does each one say?
What do these sources agree on?
Which source is the most famous?
Summarize all sources into one smooth paragraph
questions.explanation: Lesson 13: the tool's default is to produce the smoothest text with no visible contradictions, so you must force the disagreement out) 'Where do these sources disagree?': because a decision usually rests on a difference.

questions.question: Lesson 2 explains that a long response tends to drift in quality. What is the reason?
options: The model gets tired and loses focus over time
The model runs out of disk space as it writes
Each token is predicted probabilistically, so small errors accumulate over a long reply
The model stops predicting and starts guessing randomly after a fixed length
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 notes that because each token is a probability, tiny errors compound over a long reply) roughly a thousand small errors can accumulate. The first half tends to be tighter than the later half.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Building a Shared Team Playbook and Prompt Library", what is a team playbook as distinct from the prompt library?
options: The written agreement on how the team uses AI at all: tone, which tasks are handed to a tool, where data may go, and who checks what, while the library holds the working examples
A record of every prompt each person wrote privately
A tool that enforces permissions on AI usage
A report counting how many AI tasks the team ran
questions.explanation: The lesson says the playbook is the standards and the library is the working examples of those standards, and that together they turn private experiments into a common resource.

questions.question: What does the lesson say a cheat sheet is, as opposed to a lesson?
options: A condensed version of the lessons you can read to learn the skills cold
A cue that reminds you of a skill you already know, so you do not forget to apply it when the pressure is on
A collection of long worked examples
A glossary of AI terminology
questions.explanation: The lesson says each line exists to remind you of a skill you already know, and if a line needs a paragraph of explanation to be understood, it does not belong on the sheet.

questions.question: What caution does Lesson 11 draw from the HBR example about AI summaries?
options: AI summaries always catch the most important data point
AI output gravitates to the most familiar, defensible ideas and can miss a critical shift
AI summaries are too long to be useful
AI should never be used for internal summaries
questions.explanation: Lesson 11 cites HBR research that AI output gravitates to the most familiar, defensible ideas. In the president example, the AI flagged supplier costs while the team nearly missed a sales mix shift.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say good individual habits stop being enough once a team standardizes on a tool?
options: Because individual habits are usually wrong

Because habits travel with one person while a policy has to travel with the team, and once a team leans on a tool for real work it becomes an organizational purchase whether or not anyone formally bought it
Because written policies are legally required in most jurisdictions
Because tools change too fast for habits to survive
questions.explanation: The lesson makes the conversion argument and then names the failure it prevents: a company depending on tools nobody evaluated and data nobody vetted, because people signed up with a work email on their own.

questions.question: What does the lesson say follows from framing a session around a deliverable?
options: That the tool can be trusted to set the quality bar
That checks can be dropped when a deadline is tight
That the quality bar is set by the reader, so review and truth checking are not optional extras, and the stop lines matter from the first word you type
That the task must be short enough to fit in one prompt
questions.explanation: The lesson says that as soon as the output is something a person relies on, what you paste in and what you let the tool decide become questions with stakes.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say the order of the toolkit is the whole game?
options: Because the tool requires the steps in a specific interface order
Because each stage hands its output to the next, so briefing before drafting, drafting before iterating, and iterating before reviewing means each stage makes the following one easier
Because the order determines the cost of the model calls
Because reviewing a raw first draft is the most efficient use of review pass one
questions.explanation: The lesson says the skills are not a menu to pick from but an order of operations, and that reviewing a raw first draft wastes pass one, which is meant to fix a draft that already resembles the target.

questions.question: According to Lesson 4, where does AI genuinely fail?
options: Drafting, rewriting, and brainstorming
Single-right-answer facts, current or private information, and decisions with stakes
Summarizing long documents
Explaining concepts in plain language
questions.explanation: Lesson 4 says AI is good at drafting, rewriting, brainstorming, summarizing, and explaining, but fails at single-right-answer facts (numbers, dates, prices), current or private information, and decisions with real stakes.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Responsible Use: Data Policy, Vendor Evaluation, and Accountability", what are the three parts of responsible use at this scale?
options: A data policy that says what is allowed into the tool, vendor evaluation that says how you choose the tool, and accountability that says who answers when something goes wrong
Encryption, backups, and periodic access reviews
Training, licensing, and a support ticket queue
Prompt hygiene, output review, and server logging
questions.explanation: The lesson names those three pieces directly and frames them as the honest price of relying on the tool for work that involves clients, contracts, and other people's data.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Spotting the Automatable Tasks in Your Own Job", which question actually pays off?
options: Not whether your job is automatable, but which of the tasks in your job are automatable
Whether your whole occupation can be fully automated
Which of your colleagues' jobs are automatable
Whether the tool is cheaper than hiring someone
questions.explanation: The lesson says asking whether your job is automatable is too big to be useful, because a job is a bundle of dozens of small recurring tasks and only some of them are automatable.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Knowing When NOT to Use AI", which question should you start from?
options: Not "can I use AI for this," but "should I," because the answer to "can I" is almost always yes
"Can I use AI for this," because capability is the deciding factor
"Will the tool save money," regardless of the risk
"Has a competitor already automated this"
questions.explanation: The lesson says starting from can-I misleads you, because the tool can produce a draft for nearly anything you describe, which tells you nothing about whether you should use it.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Low-Risk Ways to Start Automating, and When to Stop", what one rule carries the lesson?
options: Automate the reversible, keep the human on the irreversible
Automate the most frequent task first, whatever its reversibility
Automate everything at once and review the output weekly
Never automate any step that produces an email
questions.explanation: The lesson presents that sentence as the whole filter and says almost every low-risk decision follows from it, promoting steps one at a time and demoting them just as freely.

questions.question: According to Lesson 8, when should you 'rephrase' rather than edit the existing answer?
options: When the answer is mostly correct and only needs a small fix
When the request misfired and you should say it differently rather than edit the answer
When the answer is too long and needs shortening
When the answer contains an invented fact you want to keep
questions.explanation: Lesson 8 distinguishes: refine means one targeted change on an otherwise correct answer; rephrase means the request itself misfired, so you say it differently rather than edit the output.

questions.question: The lesson says most people who think they lost an AI skill actually lost what?
options: Their motivation to keep practicing
A stack of perishable details: they memorized the wrong version of the tool and stopped checking it
Access to the tools they used before
The ability to write for an audience
questions.explanation: The lesson says the fix is not to re-learn AI but to separate the durable from the perishable, keep updating the perishable, and trust the durable to carry the load.

questions.question: Lesson 5 describes a litmus test for what is safe to put in a tool. What is it?
options: If the vendor's CEO approved the tool, anything is fine
If you would not want it printed on the front page of a trade magazine, it does not go into a public AI tool
If the data is less than a year old, it is always safe
If it fits in a single sentence, it is always safe
questions.explanation: Lesson 5's litmus test: if you would not want it printed on the front page of a trade magazine, it does not belong in a public AI tool. It also distinguishes consumer tools from enterprise tools with DPAs and no-training promises.

questions.question: What is the core rule Lesson 5 gives for anything you type into a public AI tool?
options: Assume the vendor cannot read it at all
Treat it as something the vendor could read and, depending on the tool, use later
Only enter data if it is less than 100 characters
Assume all public tools are fully encrypted and private
questions.explanation: Lesson 5 says to treat anything you type into an AI tool as something the vendor could read and, depending on the tool, use later. Stanford HAI found all six major companies trained on user conversations by default.

questions.question: Per the lesson "The Manager's Guide: Running a Company-wide Rollout", what is a rollout?
options: The deliberate, sequenced effort to spread a proven way of working across an organization beyond the people who built and tested it, while keeping the quality and controls that made it worth spreading
Giving everyone a license to the tool
A training video every employee must watch
Replacing the pilot team with a central AI department
questions.explanation: The lesson defines it as not let everyone have the tool, but let everyone use the tool the way the pilot proved works.

questions.question: Lesson 10's worked template keeps a stable instruction while facts change. What is a key step in building such a template?
options: Let the model invent any missing facts
Circle what changes between uses and keep the stable instruction fixed, then add guardrails like one filled example
Rewrite the instruction every time the facts change
Remove all formatting from the prompt
questions.explanation: Lesson 10's build steps: collect examples, circle what changes, keep the stable instruction, and add guardrails including a filled example. Name variables for meaning, not position.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Simple Repeatable Workflows You Can Run Weekly", what distinguishes a workflow from a prompt?
options: A prompt is one request, while a workflow is a fixed sequence of steps run in order toward a recurring result
A workflow requires software, while a prompt does not
A prompt produces better output than a workflow
A workflow has no output that needs checking
questions.explanation: The lesson draws the line plainly: a prompt is a single request, while a workflow is several requests arranged so each step hands its output to the next.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Putting It Together: a Real Task, End to End, Using the Whole Toolkit", what is an end-to-end session?
options: One task taken from receiving the work to producing the finished result you would hand to someone, with an AI tool as one participant throughout and you in control at every step
A single prompt that produces the whole deliverable at once
A session in which you use every feature the tool offers
A full working day spent with AI tools
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the phrase to set a scope: you are not doing a piece of the task, a first draft, or a summary, you are completing the deliverable.

questions.question: Lesson 9 names three AI failure modes. Which are they?
options: Too long, too short, and too slow
Vague asks, invented facts, and wrong formats
Spelling errors, grammar errors, and punctuation
Refusals, censorship, and repetition
questions.explanation: Lesson 9's three failure modes are the vague ask (missing role/task/context), the invented fact (specific but unverifiable), and the wrong format (you never specified the shape).

questions.question: In the worked client email, what line does Lesson 11 say is critical to include in the prompt?
options: Make the email as long and detailed as possible
Do not add any numbers, dates, or promises I did not give you
Invent a positive reason for any delay
Address the email to the CEO
questions.explanation: Lesson 11's worked example includes the leave-out line 'Do not add any numbers, dates, or promises I did not give you' to prevent the tool from inventing facts, and warns never to send unverified numbers.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say a written bar beats a shared vibe?
options: Because written standards are required by compliance frameworks
Because a confident-sounding draft gets approved faster than a careful one that is genuinely wrong, and a written bar turns the check from a feeling into a list
Because written standards let you skip review on low-priority work
Because it removes the need for an accountable owner
questions.explanation: The lesson lists what goes wrong without a written bar: the check becomes whatever each person notices, people argue about acceptability, and a miss teaches nothing because there is no standard to point at.

questions.question: Which of these would Lesson 5 consider off-limits for a public AI tool?
options: Trade secrets and unreleased proprietary information
A generic request for help drafting a public-facing email
A question about a common public holiday date
A request for synonyms of a common word
questions.explanation: Lesson 5's off-limits list includes client personal data, health and financial information, trade secrets, credentials and passwords, and unreleased proprietary information.

questions.question: According to Lesson 7, what does adding context help the model do, beyond just answering?
options: It makes the model memorize the prompt permanently
It helps the model generalize to the right answer rather than the average one
It makes the output faster by removing detail
It has no effect and only adds token cost
questions.explanation: Lesson 7 notes why-context helps generalization: with the actual facts, audience, purpose, and constraints supplied, the model produces a relevant answer instead of a generic average one.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous, per Lesson 12, to ship a draft that has been edited but not reviewed?
options: Editing makes the draft longer and harder to read
A beautifully edited draft can still be completely wrong, and it looks done so it ships on autopilot
Reviewing makes the draft worse
Editing is not a real skill
questions.explanation: Lesson 12: 'A draft can be beautifully edited and completely wrong.' The edited draft looks done, so the reviewing gate gets skipped and the error sails through underneath the tightened sentence.

questions.question: What does the lesson call an exception rule?
options: A rule that exempts managers from review
A rule letting the tool skip the quality bar for internal work
A written trigger for when output needs more than one pair of eyes, such as anything that states a price, promises a date, touches a contract, or goes to an angry customer
A rule that auto-approves drafts that pass a first check
questions.explanation: The lesson says the exception rule turns whether someone should check this from a judgment call made at midnight into a list agreed on in daylight.

questions.question: How does Lesson 3 define an AI hallucination, following IBM?
options: A short, obviously broken sentence that is easy to spot by its grammar
Output that sounds plausible but is factually wrong, irrelevant, or entirely fabricated
A rare error that only happens on obscure trivia questions
A software bug that will be patched in the next update
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 uses IBM's definition: output that sounds plausible but is factually wrong, irrelevant, or entirely fabricated. It also debunks the myths that hallucinations only hit obscure trivia or are a fixable bug.

questions.question: What is the single biggest lever in AI research, per Lesson 13?
options: Asking the tool what the industry says about a topic
Giving the tool the actual documents to work from instead of asking it to recall information
Asking for a longer, more detailed summary
Letting the tool search the internet on its own
questions.explanation: Lesson 13: the single biggest lever is giving the tool the actual documents (grounding/RAG) rather than asking it to produce information from memory, which lowers the risk of hallucinations.

questions.question: How does the lesson distinguish a workflow from automation?
options: Automation always requires writing code, while a workflow does not
A workflow runs on a schedule and automation runs on demand
In a workflow you are always at the check, while automation is a step that runs and checks itself, with you verifying less often or not at all
A workflow cannot draw on saved prompts
questions.explanation: The lesson states the difference is where your attention has to go: a workflow waits for you at the check, while automation is a step you deliberately promote from human-in-the-loop so the check can be left.

questions.question: What is a 'premortem,' as Lesson 16 describes it?
options: A checklist of required tasks before a project starts
A stress-testing technique where you imagine the project has already failed and work backwards to explain why
A review of the project after it finishes
A financial forecast of project costs
questions.explanation: Lesson 16 cites Gary Klein's premortem: instead of asking 'what could go wrong,' you imagine the project has already failed and work backwards) prospective hindsight that makes it safe to name problems early.

questions.question: How should you handle a number or fact the tool produces that is not in the sources you provided?
options: Use it, because the tool is usually right
Drop it and only use claims that trace to a source you gave the tool
Ask the tool to make it more specific
Merge it with the sources to make a new claim
questions.explanation: Lesson 13's rule: every claim you use points to a source you gave the tool, and you check the ones that matter against that source. In the worked example, an invented '92 percent satisfaction' number was dropped.

questions.question: Why does the lesson argue for versioning shared prompts?
options: So the library can be audited for compliance
So usage can be billed back to each team
Because one person tweaking a shared prompt for their own scenario can break it for everyone else, and without versions nobody can get the old one back
Because version numbers make the prompts run faster
questions.explanation: The lesson says versioning matters more the more people touch a shared prompt, and names the exact failure mode: a private tweak breaks the prompt for the rest of the team with no way to roll back.

questions.question: How does Lesson 6 say you should verify a claim the AI makes?
options: Ask another AI tool to confirm it
Trust it if the AI states it confidently
Verify against a primary source, never another AI
Accept it if it is written in a professional tone
questions.explanation: Lesson 6 teaches verification against a primary source using lateral reading, never by asking another AI. The confidence trap means a certain tone is 'just how the tool talks,' not evidence of truth.

questions.question: The lesson distinguishes a model from automation. Which statement captures that difference?
options: Automation produces unpredictable output, while a model follows fixed rules
A model makes judgments and is inherently unpredictable, while automation executes pre-written rules
A model and automation are the same thing with different names
Automation requires judgment, while a model never varies in its output
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 frames the key difference: automation follows pre-written rules, while a model applies judgment and is inherently unpredictable) which is why its outputs need checking.

questions.question: Why does Lesson 15 say the verification of extracted action items is not optional?
options: Because the tool's list is usually too short
Because a wrong action item is a broken promise and a strained client relationship, not just a wrong number
Because action items are less important than the agenda
Because the transcript is not needed after the meeting
questions.explanation: Lesson 15: a wrong action item puts a person on the hook for something they never said yes to. The cost is a broken promise and a strained relationship, so you must confirm each item was actually agreed, with the right owner and deadline.
